orders.description: Dutchess County order dated February 17, 2011, insofar as appealed from
orders.trial_court_action: Granted the institute’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Johnson, a Janitronics employee, alleged that she slipped on a wet hallway floor near a landing and stairwell while working in the institute’s building. She thought the floor had just been mopped.

legal_issues.finding: Johnson testified that an institute employee told her another employee had mopped the area. On the owner’s motion, that account left a triable question whether the owner created the wet condition.
The court stated the owner’s initial burden concerning actual notice. Its case-specific analysis concerned creation and constructive notice.
The institute supplied no evidence of the last inspection or mopping before the accident.
The owner did not meet its initial burden, so the sufficiency of Johnson’s opposition did not affect the disposition.

evidence_discussed.description: The institute relied principally on Johnson’s deposition describing the wet floor and her identification of the employees involved in the reported mopping.

quality.notes: The institute is expressly identified as owner of the building, but the supplied opinion does not establish its private or public status. The appeal concerns the direct premises claim, not a third-party-only dispute.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals, as limited by her brief, from so much of an or *1078 der of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Pagones, J.), dated February 17, 2011, as granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

On August 10, 2007, the plaintiff, an employee of the third-party defendant, Janitronics, allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on a wet floor while working in a building owned by the defendant.
The plaintiff appeals, and we reverse.

A defendant who moves for summary judgment in a slip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the hazardous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it

In support of its motion for summary judgment, the defendant relied principally upon the plaintiff’s deposition testimony. In that testimony, the plaintiff stated that she slipped and fell on a wet portion of a hallway in an area of the defendant’s building near a landing and stairwell. It appeared to her that the floor had just been mopped.
She was sure, from dealing with these two people in the past, that they were, in fact, employees of the defendant and not employees of the company for which *1079 she worked.
this person advised her that another employee of the defendant, whom the plaintiff could only recall as a “Mexican” person, had mopped that area.
Under the facts as testified to by the plaintiff, the defendant failed to establish that it did not create the condition complained of

Furthermore, the defendant failed to meet its burden of demonstrating the absence of constructive notice of the dangerous condition since it failed to submit any evidence as to when the floor was last inspected or mopped prior to the plaintiffs accident

Since the defendant failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to whether it created the condition complained of or had notice of the condition complained of, it failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint should have been denied, regardless of the sufficiency of the opposing papers

orders.trial_court_action: Granted Stop & Shop’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Loper alleged that she tripped over a plastic container of mums outside the supermarket. She suggested wind had moved it into her path and testified that she had not seen it there about 15 minutes earlier.

legal_issues.finding: The supermarket established prima facie that it did not create the condition, and Loper raised no triable issue.
The court accepted the store’s showing that it lacked actual notice.
The store showed a lack of constructive notice. Its submissions included Loper’s account of passing the site about 15 minutes earlier without seeing the condition.

evidence_discussed.description: Loper’s deposition described her earlier passage through the same area.

quality.notes: Movement of the pot by wind was Loper’s supposition. The record does not identify when or how it actually came to be in her path.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Denise F. Molia, J.), dated November 18, 2020. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell on a plastic container of mums on the exterior grounds of the defendant's supermarket in Riverhead.
surmising that wind must have blown the potted flowers from its display location and into her path.
Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that it did not create the alleged hazardous condition or have actual or constructive notice of its existence

transcripts of the plaintiff's deposition testimony, in which she testified that when she traversed the accident site approximately 15 minutes prior to the incident, she did not see the condition that subsequently caused her to trip and fall.
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted both the owner’s and the management defendants’ motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Murphy rented an apartment in the building. In October 2011 she slipped on steps leading down from the back porch. She said a slippery green substance on the porch transferred to her shoes before she reached the steps.

legal_issues.finding: Murphy’s limited obligation to clear debris and snow did not necessarily displace responsibility for an apparently shared porch. Even if it was not shared, defendants retained rights of entry, inspection and repair.

Defendants knew of the earlier condition and presented evidence it had been cleaned. Murphy’s account of repeated complaints and the caseworker’s corroboration raised a triable issue of notice of its persistence.
Evidence that the condition persisted after cleaning raised a triable question whether defendants had notice.
Murphy countered the defense showing that cleaning had resolved the condition with evidence of persistence, repeated complaints and the substance on the porch.

The photographs showed the substance on the porch, not the steps. Murphy explained how she had picked it up on her shoes. The court found the affidavit consistent with her deposition; any discrepancies concerned credibility.
Differences in clarity between Murphy’s affidavit and deposition did not permit the court to resolve credibility on summary judgment.

evidence_discussed.description: Murphy described persistence and complaints; Martin and Hiscox denied receiving later complaints and described the cleaning.
The caseworker’s affidavit and deposition corroborated Murphy’s account.
Murphy’s photographs depicted the substance on portions of the porch but not on the steps.
The lease assigned limited porch-clearing responsibilities to Murphy and reserved inspection and repair rights.

quality.notes: The appellate court denied both motions in one reversed order. It did not conclusively find the porch was a common area or that the substance caused the fall.

evidence.quote: Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Krogmann, J.), entered May 14, 2014 in Warren County, which granted defendants’ motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Plaintiff rented an apartment in a building owned by defendant Jeffrey Hiscox and managed on behalf of defendant Hometown Real Estate by defendant Andrew Martin. The building has an exterior back porch accessible from the first floor apartments and, in October 2011, plaintiff slipped and fell on steps leading down from it.
Plaintiff then commenced this premises liability action, alleging that her fall was caused by a slippery green substance on the porch that could and should have been addressed by defendants.
Plaintiff now appeals, and we reverse.

Plaintiff was required by the lease to “properly care for the” porch area by keeping it clear of debris and snow, but it is doubtful that her limited duties in that regard absolved de *1127 fendants of their general responsibility to maintain a seemingly common area accessible by other tenants

even assuming that the porch was not a common area, defendants reserved the right to enter the premises leased by plaintiff for inspection and repair purposes and, as such, may be held “liable for failure to repair a dangerous condition” therein if they were on notice of it

Here, Martin and Hiscox were both aware that there was “green slime” on the porch around the time that plaintiff rented the apartment in May 2011. Hiscox authorized Martin to hire a contractor to clean the porch, which was done, and Martin stated that he did not observe the substance on his subsequent visits to the property. Martin and Hiscox, moreover, both denied receiving any complaints about the condition of the porch after that time.

Given this prima facie showing that the condition had been resolved and that defendants lacked actual or constructive notice of a continuing risk, plaintiff became obliged to come forward with proof that a “recurring dangerous condition existed in the area of the accident which was routinely left unaddressed by” defendants
Plaintiff averred that the green substance had persisted after the porch was cleaned, that it was slippery when wet and that her repeated demands for Martin to fix the problem went unaddressed.

Those assertions were corroborated by the affidavit and deposition testimony of caseworker Allison Sullivan, who had assisted plaintiff with her living arrangements and had also attempted to raise the issue with Martin.

Plaintiff further submitted photographs of the area that show the substance on portions of the porch — albeit not on the steps themselves — and *1128 stated that she fell after “picking] up” the substance on her shoes as she walked across the porch.

While plaintiff’s affidavit was clearer than her opaque deposition testimony in explaining the exact mechanism of her fall, the two are not contradictory, and whatever discrepancies exist between them raised credibility questions that cannot be answered in the summary judgment context

Thus, because plaintiff provided more than “mere speculation” to suggest that defendants had actual or constructive notice of the condition that caused her fall, the motions for summary judgment should have been denied
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and motions denied.

orders.description: New York County order entered August 29, 2016
orders.trial_court_action: Denied Macy’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Ahmed alleged that he slipped on an escalator in Macy’s department store. He testified that the rubber handrail pulled up as he grasped it while slipping. His wife’s statement described the stairs as wet.

legal_issues.finding: The maintenance and inspection history showed no prior reports of accidents or escalator problems, and the record contained no prior complaint about the handrail.
Neither the wife’s hearsay statement about wet stairs nor Ahmed’s handrail testimony showed how long either alleged condition existed.
The engineer’s opinion that the wooden treads were more slippery than industry standards permitted did not raise a triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Macy’s submitted two employees’ depositions. The wife’s statement about wet stairs was characterized as hearsay.
Ahmed described the movement of the handrail as he slipped.
The escalator maintenance records supported the regular servicing and lack of prior reports.
Thyssenkrupp and city records documented regular escalator maintenance and inspections.
Ahmed’s engineer addressed the slipperiness of the wooden treads.

quality.notes: The court granted Macy’s motion only. The record mentions alternative alleged conditions but does not identify one as the established cause.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Geoffrey D.S. Wright, J.), entered August 29, 2016, which denied the motion of defendant Macy's Inc. for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, and the motion granted.
The Clerk is directed to enter judgment accordingly.
plaintiff alleges that he was injured when he slipped and fell on an escalator in Macy's department store.
Macy's established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law

Macy's submitted, inter alia, deposition testimony of two of its employees, as well as the records of maintenance and inspections of the escalator by defendant Thyssenkrupp Corp. and the New York City Department of Buildings.

Such evidence showed that the escalator was regularly maintained and inspected during the years prior to plaintiff's accident, and there were never any reports of accidents or other problems with the escalator
Plaintiff's wife's hearsay statement that the stairs were wet does not indicate that they were wet long enough for Macy's to have notice of the condition.

plaintiff's testimony that the rubber handrail pulled up when he grasped at it as he slipped, does not raise an issue of fact that any such defect existed long enough for Macy's to have notice, particularly since there were no prior complaints and in light of the evidence of regular maintenance and City inspections showing no problems
Furthermore, the opinion of plaintiff's expert engineer that the wooden escalator treads were more slippery than industry safety standards permit does not raise an issue of fact.

orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Robustelli allegedly slipped in the laundry room of a building owned by Westchester Towers Owners Corp. and managed by Prime Locations. The opinion does not specify the hazard.

legal_issues.finding: The owner and manager showed that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition.
Defendants established lack of actual notice, and Robustelli raised no triable factual issue.
The defense likewise established lack of constructive notice.
The defense failed to show that Robustelli did not know the cause of her fall. Its successful ground for dismissal was separate.

quality.notes: No substance, inspection details or evidence type are identified in this opinion. The rejection of the unidentified-cause argument did not prevent dismissal.

evidence.quote: the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Lefkowitz, J.), dated September 10, 2014, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell in the laundry room of a building owned by the defendant Westchester Towers Owners Corp., and managed by the defendant Prime Locations, Inc.
Contrary to the defendants' contention, they failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to slip and fall

However, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition that caused the plaintiff to slip and fall or have actual or constructive notice of its existence
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
